scenes.heading: Atomic structure
scenes.sub: Why do neon signs glow red?
scenes.say: Why does a neon sign glow red, and why does each metal give its own flame colour? The answer lies in how electrons are arranged around the nucleus.

scenes.heading: Inside the atom
points: Nucleus: protons (+1) and neutrons (0)
Electrons (−1) outside, about 1/1836 of a proton
Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = p + n
Isotopes: same Z, different neutrons
Aᵣ = Σ (fractional abundance × isotopic mass)
scenes.say: Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus, with tiny electrons outside. Z counts protons, and A counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different neutrons, so they react the same way. The relative atomic mass is an abundance-weighted average.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A lift stops at level 1, 2 or 3, never at level 2.4
scenes.science: An electron's energy is quantised: only levels n = 1, 2, 3 …
scenes.breaks: an electron has no exact path between floors. The levels describe energies, not places.
scenes.say: Energy levels are like floors in a shopping centre. The lift stops at level one, two or three, never two point four. Electron energy is quantised the same way. Dropping a floor gives out exactly that energy difference as one photon, so we see sharp lines, not a rainbow.
scenes.caption: Energy levels are like floors in a shopping centre. The lift stops at level 1, 2 or 3, never 2.4. Electron energy is quantised the same way. Dropping a floor gives out exactly that energy difference as one photon, so we see sharp lines, not a rainbow.

scenes.heading: Photon energy
scenes.say: A photon's energy is h times its frequency, or h c over the wavelength. So shorter wavelength means bigger energy. Ultraviolet photons carry more energy than visible light, which carries more than infrared.
scenes.caption: A photon's energy is E = hν = hc/λ. So shorter wavelength means bigger energy. UV photons carry more energy than visible light, which carries more than infrared.

scenes.heading: Worked example: hydrogen's red line
scenes.question: Find the wavelength of light emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2.
scenes.say: When hydrogen's electron drops from level three to level two, the Bohr formula gives an energy of three point zero two eight times ten to the minus nineteen joules. Wavelength equals h c over delta E: six hundred and fifty-six nanometres, a red line.
scenes.caption: When hydrogen's electron drops from n = 3 to n = 2, the Bohr formula gives ΔE = 3.028 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. λ = hc/ΔE = 656 nm, a red line.

scenes.heading: Bohr model vs quantum model

left.title: Bohr model
points: Electron on a fixed circular orbit
Works for hydrogen and one-electron ions
Fails for many-electron atoms

right.title: Quantum model
points: Electron described by a wavefunction ψ
ψ² gives probability density
Orbital = region of space, not a path

scenes.say: Bohr's model explains hydrogen, but fails for atoms with more than one electron, and the uncertainty principle rules out a precise orbit. The quantum model uses a wavefunction. Psi squared gives probability, so an orbital is a cloud, not a path.
scenes.caption: Bohr's model explains hydrogen, but fails for atoms with more than one electron, and the uncertainty principle rules out a precise orbit. The quantum model uses a wavefunction. ψ² gives probability, so an orbital is a cloud, not a path.

scenes.heading: Quantum numbers
points: n = 1, 2, 3 … (shell, size, energy)
l = 0 to n − 1 (s, p, d, f: shape)
mₗ = −l to +l (orientation)
mₛ = +½ or −½ (electron spin)
s, p, d, f have 1, 3, 5, 7 orbitals
scenes.say: n starts at one. l runs from zero to n minus one, giving s, p, d and f. m l runs from minus l to plus l, and spin is plus or minus a half. So s, p, d and f hold one, three, five and seven orbitals.
scenes.caption: n starts at 1. l runs from 0 to n − 1, giving s, p, d and f. mₗ runs from −l to +l, and spin is +½ or −½. So s, p, d and f hold 1, 3, 5 and 7 orbitals.

points: Isotopes: same Z, different neutrons
Line spectra prove energy is quantised
E = hν = hc/λ
Orbital = probability cloud (ψ²), not a path
An orbital has n − 1 nodes in total
scenes.say: Quick recap. Isotopes differ only in neutrons. Line spectra show energy is quantised. E equals h c over lambda. An orbital is a probability cloud with n minus one nodes. Now try the practice questions!
